newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela CANTV issue expectations seen too high.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela CANTV issue expectations seen too high.

text.p: When Venezuela sold a controlling 40 percent stake in telephone company CANTV in 1991, investors had to push past a local congressman who had literally wrapped himself in the national flag outside the bidding room.

The planned global share issue of the government's remaining 49 percent stake in CANTV set for mid-November has roused far less nationalistic fervor but expectations surrounding the sale may still be dangerously high, analysts said.

Official forecasts that the share price will be similar to the $4.71 set in 1991 appear far-fetched given that CANTV's monopoly on basic line services now has just four years to run. Control of the company, won by a GTE Corp -led consortium in 1991, is not on offer this time.
"It seems clear that the price will be lower than that paid in 1991," said Alfredo Bozo, Latin American equities trader with Credit Lyonnais in New York.
Politicians have already warned that the state's CANTV shares cannot be sold "for the price of a skinny chicken."
"The magic number is $4 (per share). Below $4 you get into all sorts of political problems," said Alex Dalmady of the local Invest Analysis consultants.

Legislators have also stressed that locals must get a fair share of the global offering. The government, accordingly, set aside nine percent of the company for workers and between five and 10 percent for local capital markets.
A further 11 percent of shares offered to workers on easy terms in 1991 could also enter the market for the first time.
"It's a big issue for Venezuela...It will definitely become the market's benchmark," said Bozo.
The weight of CANTV should tip the balance and provide the local market with the critical liquidity levels needed to attract foreign investors.

"Most companies in Venezuela are family-owned so this is one more important company moving onto the exchange. It would also be another company among the small universe of shares that large investment funds can move into," said one New York-based analyst. Indeed, the mere anticipation of the CANTV listing and its impact on the local market has contributed to an extraordinary run of eight record-breaking sessions on the Caracas Stock Exchange in recent days.

But some analysts fear that the local market, whose capitalization is still less than $6 billion, will not be able to absorb the CANTV shares. Others are concerned that the issue will drag the market down, as investors sell off other stocks to buy into the offering.
After the listing, analysts question CANTV's medium term prospects.
CANTV has come a long way since 1991, raising line density from about 7.5 per 100 inhabitants in 1991 to about 12 per 100 inhabitants now, respectable by Latin American standards.
By comparison, Telefonica de Peru's, whose 23.6 percent share offering in July was massively oversubscribed, has a line density of about five per 100 inhabitants.
Indeed, CANTV recently announced it would slow down the rate of new line installations due to "over-saturation" of the market.
While CANTV has exceed concession requirements on line installations, plans to reduce cross-subsidies of local calls by international and long-distance calls are lagging.
Meanwhile potential competitors, which will surely compete with CANTV for lucrative long-distance and international services in 2001, are already gaining footholds in the local market.
The CANTV issue has also been billed by many as the defining moment in an economic reform program launched in April with backing from the International Monetary Fund.

"Its listing will add credibility to the privatization program, spotlight Venezuela and provide an indication of the path that future reforms in Venezuela will follow," said Santiago Millan with Caspian Securities in New York.
But others question whether much could be read into a successful CANTV sale.
"The hard part was done in 1991," said one local analyst, who said other privatizations of heavy industries and state banks scheduled for later this year will face far tougher opposition.
-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600
